tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on What Is Sociology?

questions.question: Explain the difference between sociology and common sense, using examples.
questions.correctAnswer: Sociology uses systematic research and evidence; common sense relies on untested assumptions. Example: common sense says 'criminals are born'; sociology shows crime is influenced by poverty, socialisation and labelling. Sociology challenges taken-for-granted assumptions.

questions.question: Describe what C. Wright Mills meant by the sociological imagination.
questions.correctAnswer: The sociological imagination sees the connection between personal experiences and wider social forces. Example: divorce may feel like a personal failure, but rising divorce rates reflect social changes (changing gender roles, easier divorce laws, declining stigma). Mills argued we need this imagination to understand society.

questions.question: Evaluate whether individual behaviour is shaped more by social structures or personal agency.
questions.correctAnswer: Structure: social institutions (family, education, economy) shape our choices - working-class children are less likely to attend university. Agency: individuals make choices within constraints - some working-class children do succeed. questions.correctAnswer: A grade 9 response will: define sociology and common sense; argue they overlap (both make claims about society); argue they differ fundamentally (sociology uses evidence, challenges assumptions, reveals hidden patterns); give examples where common sense is wrong (crime rates, educational achievement, gender roles); conclude: while sociology and common sense both describe society, sociology is fundamentally different because it is systematic, evidence-based, and challenges assumptions that common sense accepts uncritically.
